ogTitle: Yom Chinda Old Street, Rayong — Century-Old Houses, Cafes, Local Food
ogDesc: Rayong's very first street, with old wooden shophouses lined along the river, a small museum, cafes inside a nobleman's home, and local food. Walkable in half a day.
intro: Yom Chinda Road was the first proper street in Rayong, and the old trading quarter that locals once called the town's 'Beverly Hills'. Today century-old Sino-Portuguese wooden houses still line the Rayong River — some now run as small museums, some have turned into cafes, and the rest are still real family homes. You can walk the whole street comfortably in half a day.

blocks.html: If you've got a free half-day in Rayong, Yom Chinda Road is worth a walk — and not because it's some old quarter dressed up for tourists. It was the town's first street and once its trading hub, with rice mills, a cinema, a boatyard, and rows of Chinese merchant shophouses. Plenty of the wooden houses are still lived in today, mixed in with newer shops, which gives the street more of a real, lived-in feel than the old districts that have become pure photo backdrops.

The street is short — you can do it in a single straight walk, running parallel to the Rayong River. The draw is the architecture: wooden and masonry buildings in the Sino-Portuguese style, an old nobleman's house, a Chinese shrine, and shops that have slowly opened up over the years. We've lined up the stops worth pausing at in walking order.

blocks.text: Walking past the old houses and the nobleman's mansion

blocks.html: The heart of Yom Chinda is its old wooden houses. Some are teak homes in a Thai-Chinese style, others are brick shophouses in the Sino-Portuguese mold, with fretwork, wooden louvre shutters, and faded old shop signs. Walk slowly and look closely at the facades. Many of these houses are still occupied, so photograph them respectfully and keep the owners in mind.

items.name: Rayong City Museum (Baan Sat-udom)
items.blurb: A small museum inside the home of Khun Si Uthaikhet, who once owned the town's rice mill, cinema, and boatyard. It displays old photos, household objects, and the stories behind this street. Free entry, open 9am–6pm daily.

items.name: Chinese shrine on the street
items.blurb: An old shrine that reflects the Thai-Chinese community who were the pioneering merchants of this quarter. Stop in to make an offering and look at the traditional Chinese architecture.

items.name: Riverside wooden houses
items.blurb: Near the end of the street you can walk through to the Rayong River, where some wooden houses turn their backs to the water in the old community style. A nice spot for photos in the late afternoon.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Most of the museums and shops close on certain days or open late. If you're here mainly for the buildings and the museum, come late morning to afternoon on a Friday through Sunday, when the most shops are open.

blocks.text: Cafes inside the old wooden houses

blocks.html: One of Yom Chinda's charms is that several old houses have been renovated into cafes while keeping the original timber frames and atmosphere — you really can sip coffee inside a century-old shophouse. Here are the ones people talk about most that are still open.

items.name: Laan Ek Coffeehouse
items.blurb: A part-cafe, part-gallery in a building over a hundred years old. Downstairs is for coffee and snacks; upstairs has art and old photos of the town. Photographers love it for the light and the old structural bones.

items.name: Old House At Yomjinda
items.blurb: A two-storey wooden cafe done up in warm wood tones with a nostalgic feel and a skylight that lets the daylight in. Drinks and bakery items. A popular stop to rest between stretches of the walk.
items.meta: Open daily (double-check hours on their page) · Yom Chinda Road

items.name: Ya Chindom
items.blurb: A Thai-dessert cafe in an old wooden house with a quiet, calm atmosphere — good for tea and Thai sweets. If you like traditional Thai desserts served in an old home, this is your spot.

items.name: Raan Choei
items.blurb: A small cafe with a red telephone box out front as a photo prop. It serves Thai tea, cocoa, coffee, and Thai mains, with old photos and original furniture upstairs.
items.meta: Drinks + Thai food · Yom Chinda Road

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Raan Rayong, the long-running tea house that a lot of blogs used to review, was closed for a long stretch during COVID. Check the shop's latest page before you go to make sure it's open, so you don't turn up to a locked door.

This quarter isn't just cafes — there are local eateries that Rayong people actually eat at, scattered along the street and the side lanes. Good for a lunch stop before or after you walk the buildings.

items: Jay Muay Noodles — a long-established noodle shop in the area, a light meal to break up the walk
Som Tam Anamai — a local papaya-salad shop with bold flavours, good for a Thai-style lunch
Jay Sombat Rice & Curry — point-and-pick rice and curry at easy prices, a real local spot
Baan Yom Chinda Riverside Restaurant — a proper sit-down meal with river views

blocks.html: On weekends, Yom Chinda Road runs a Walking Street in the evening, where you can eat and shop your way down the lane. There's local food, craft work, and handmade goods to browse — this is when the quarter is at its liveliest.

blocks.text: How to get there and when to go

items: Location — Yom Chinda Road, Mueang Rayong district, right in the town centre near the Rayong River. Drive or take a vehicle in, park nearby, and walk from there
Getting there — coming from Bangkok, take a car, van, or coach to Rayong town, then a taxi or motorbike into the old quarter
Best timing — late morning to afternoon, Friday to Sunday, when the most shops are open. For the Walking Street, come on a Saturday evening
Time needed — walking the buildings, visiting the museum, and stopping at one cafe takes around 2–3 hours, which is about right

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Yom Chinda doesn't take long to finish, so it pairs easily with other sights around Rayong in the same day — walk Yom Chinda in the morning, then head to Mae Ramphueng Beach or catch a boat over to Koh Samet in the afternoon.

faq.q: How long does it take to walk Yom Chinda Road?
faq.a: It's a short street you can do in one straight walk. Including the museum and a cafe stop, allow around 2–3 hours — a good half-day activity before you move on somewhere else.

faq.q: What day should I visit Yom Chinda Road?
faq.a: The shops and cafes are most open on Friday through Sunday, late morning to afternoon. If you want the Walking Street with food and craft stalls, come on a Saturday evening.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for the Rayong City Museum?
faq.a: The Rayong City Museum in Baan Sat-udom is free to enter, open daily around 9am–6pm. Just sign in and go through. It displays old photos and the story of Yom Chinda Road and Rayong town.

faq.q: Does Yom Chinda have cafes inside old wooden houses?
faq.a: Several — for example Laan Ek Coffeehouse in a century-old part-gallery building, the two-storey Old House At Yomjinda, and Ya Chindom, a Thai-dessert cafe in an old home.

faq.q: Where can I go after visiting Yom Chinda?
faq.a: Since it's quick to finish, you can pair it with other sights the same day — head to Mae Ramphueng Beach, take a boat to Koh Samet, or eat seafood at Ban Phe.
